screens.title: Collision Detection and Response
screens.narratorSegment: Collision is the foundation of interactive gameplay: it defines when actors meet, when triggers fire, and when physics reacts. In this lesson you will learn the building blocks that Unreal Engine 5 provides — simple geometric primitives for collision, collision presets and channels that filter interactions, and the two event families you use in C++: overlap and hit events. We'll also show a practical projectile example that binds OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentHit so your game can respond to triggers and physical impacts. Understanding the difference between overlap and hit matters because choosing the wrong one leads to missed events or unexpected blocking. For example, trigger volumes use overlaps so players pass through while pickups still register; walls use blocking and hits so movement is stopped and impact logic runs. By the end of this chapter you will know how to configure a component's object type and responses, enable the right event flags, and bind UFUNCTION handlers safely. Keep an eye on performance: simple shapes and smart filtering are essential. Ready to explore collision presets, event binding, and test workflows in the editor?

screens.title: Collision Primitives and UPrimitiveComponent
screens.narratorSegment: Collision primitives are the geometric building blocks Unreal uses to detect contact. The most common are spheres, boxes, and capsules, implemented as components such as USphereComponent, UBoxComponent, and UCapsuleComponent derived from UPrimitiveComponent. Choosing a primitive is a balance between semantic fit and performance: spheres and capsules give smooth bounds for characters and projectiles, boxes are cheap for static props, and complex per-triangle collision should be avoided unless necessary. A primitive attaches to an actor as a component and becomes the basis for queries and physics responses. When you set a primitive as RootComponent, it defines the actor's collision footprint; when it's a child, it augments a visual mesh for triggers or localized collision. Collision Primitives and UPrimitiveComponent means a collision primitive is a basic geometric component used to test and respond to interactions; prefer simple shapes for performance.. In practical terms, shape types, component attachment, and why shape choice matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
Collision Primitives & UPrimitiveComponent
How shape choices affect gameplay stability, queries, and performance.
What they are
  • USphereComponent: simple radial bounds, excellent for projectiles and proximity checks.
  • UBoxComponent: axis-aligned bounds, useful for triggers and static props.
  • UCapsuleComponent: common for characters — smooth rounded vertical shape prevents snagging.
Concrete example
Use a sphere for a projectile’s collision sphere so bounce and overlap checks are predictable.
Common mistake
Attaching a heavy per-poly collision mesh to many moving objects causes expensive queries and stuttering.
Key Takeaway

Prefer simple primitives for runtime collision. Use per-poly only when accuracy is required and cost is acceptable.

Primitive comparison
Sphere
Fast radial tests, good for bouncing projectiles and proximity triggers.
Box
Useful for triggers and simple static geometry; cheaper than per-triangle collision.
Capsule
Standard for character collision; reduces snagging on world edges.
Why shape choice matters
  • Performance: cheaper shapes mean fewer collision tests per frame.
  • Behavior: shapes define how objects slide, bounce, or trigger events.
  • Stability: capsules avoid corner snagging for characters.

screens.title: Collision Presets, Channels, and Object Types
screens.narratorSegment: Collision presets and channels form a matrix that determines how two components interact. A Collision Preset is a convenient predefined set of responses such as BlockAll or OverlapAll. Under the hood, each component has an Object Type and a set of responses to other channels. Collision Channels are categories you define in Project Settings; they represent semantic groups like Pawn, Projectile, WorldStatic, or Pickup. For every pair of object types the engine consults the response (Ignore, Overlap, or Block) and either performs physics, generates overlap events, or ignores the other component. This filtering is essential for performance: well-chosen channels reduce unnecessary queries and ensure only meaningful interactions are processed. For example, you can set your Projectile channel to block WorldStatic and overlap Pickup so projectiles stop at walls but pick up items when passing through. Misconfiguring responses — such as setting both sides to Ignore or both to Overlap when you need a physical block — results in missing events or unexpected pass-through behavior. Always verify both the component's Object Type and its responses in the Details panel. Collision Presets, Channels, and Object Types means use presets for quick configs and custom channels for fine-grained control. both sides' responses determine whether an event or block occurs.. In practical terms, how the collision matrix filters interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Presets, Channels, Object Types
A matrix determines how components react: Ignore, Overlap, or Block.
How to think about it
  1. Assign an Object Type to the component (e.g., Projectile or Pawn).
  2. Set Responses for other channels (Ignore/Overlap/Block).
  3. Use presets when they match your intent or create a custom channel for specific rules.
Example
Projectile: ObjectType = WorldDynamic; Response to WorldStatic = Block; Response to Pickup = Overlap.
Misconception
Setting a preset without checking object types can yield unexpected ignore behavior if the other actor's type doesn't match assumptions.

screens.title: Overlap Events: When and How to Use Them
screens.narratorSegment: Overlap events are used when actors should pass through each other while still triggering logic. They occur when components' responses to each other are set to Overlap and at least one side has Generate Overlap Events enabled. This makes overlaps ideal for trigger volumes, pickups, and zone detection. The typical process is: define a trigger component (UBoxComponent or USphereComponent), set its Object Type and Response to Overlap the target Object Type, enable Generate Overlap Events, and bind OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentEndOverlap to UFUNCTION handlers in your actor. At runtime, the engine calls your handler with references to the other actor and component so you can inspect tags, apply effects, or destroy a pickup. A common debugging step is to use the Show Collision view to verify the shapes and ensure both components have compatible responses. One misconception is assuming only the trigger needs Generate Overlap Events — sometimes the other side also needs it depending on configuration. Always confirm both sides when events don't fire. content.html:
Process Flow
Using Overlap Events
Step-by-step setup to ensure overlaps fire predictably.
  1. Choose a primitive for the trigger (UBoxComponent/USphereComponent).
  2. Set Object Type and set collision response to Overlap the relevant channel.
  3. Call SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true) on the trigger component.
  4. Bind OnComponentBeginOverlap with AddDynamic to your UFUNCTION handler.
  5. Test by entering the volume and watching the Output Log for your handler message.
Concrete Example
A pickup's UBoxComponent uses Overlap with Pawn; OnComponentBeginOverlap destroys the pickup and grants health.
Gotcha
If both sides are set to Block, you won't get overlaps; if both Overlap you won't get a Hit — choose according to intent.
Key Takeaway

Use Overlap for trigger-like behavior and confirm Generate Overlap Events and response settings on both components when debugging.

Example handler signature
UFUNCTION()
void OnOverlapBegin(UPrimitiveComponent* OverlappedComp, AActor* OtherActor,
    UPrimitiveComponent* OtherComp, int32 OtherBodyIndex, bool bFromSweep,
    const FHitResult& SweepResult);
Implement this function to inspect OtherActor and apply gameplay logic when the overlap begins.
Check these editor flags
  • Generate Overlap Events = true on the trigger component.
  • Collision Response to Pawn (or your player channel) = Overlap.
  • Player capsule's Generate Overlap Events true if needed.

screens.title: Hit Events: Physics, Blocking, and Contact
screens.narratorSegment: Hit events happen when two collision primitives physically collide and are prevented from passing through each other. They are used for impacts, projectile impacts, and physical responses like applying impulses or spawning effects. For hit events to fire, components must be configured to block each other and either simulate physics or explicitly enable Generate Hit Events / SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision. If a rigidbody is involved, Simulate Physics can trigger hits; for static or kinematic objects, SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) is often required. Implement OnComponentHit in C++ with the signature that receives NormalImpulse and an FHitResult so you can find the exact contact location and the other actor involved. A frequent misconception is thinking Overlap and Hit can both fire for the same pair — in most cases, a Block response produces hits and prevents overlap, while Overlap prevents blocking. Choose the response according to whether you want a physical block or a trigger-like notification. Use hits for damage-on-impact and physical reactions, remembering to check both components' collision responses and flags when debugging. Hit Events: Physics, Blocking, and Contact means hit events require a block response plus physics or notify flags; they provide contact details like impact location and impulse.. In practical terms, when hits fire and how to make them reliable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
OnComponentHit — Physical Contact
Use hit events for collisions that should physically stop movement or cause an impact response.
How to make hits happen
  • Ensure both components' collision responses are set to Block for each other.
  • Enable Simulate Physics on dynamic bodies, or SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) for kinematic objects.
  • Bind OnComponentHit with AddDynamic to your UFUNCTION handler.
Concrete example
A projectile hits a wall. OnComponentHit provides location and NormalImpulse so you can spawn an impact effect.
Common mistake
Forgetting to enable notify flags or simulation means the engine will not call your hit handler even though objects appear to collide.
Key Takeaway

Use hits for physical impacts. Confirm blocking responses and the appropriate notify or physics flags so contact callbacks run.

Example handler signature
UFUNCTION()
void OnHit(UPrimitiveComponent* HitComp, AActor* OtherActor, UPrimitiveComponent* OtherComp,
    FVector NormalImpulse, const FHitResult& Hit);
Use Hit.Location from FHitResult to spawn effects and NormalImpulse for physical reaction magnitude.
Editor checklist
  • Collision Enabled: Query and Physics if using physics-driven hits.
  • SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision for kinematic objects that should generate hits.
  • Confirm both sides' responses are not Ignore.

screens.title: Binding Overlap & Hit in C++ — Header
screens.narratorSegment: Binding collision delegates in C++ starts with clear declarations in your actor's header file. You declare component pointers such as USphereComponent* CollisionSphere and UProjectileMovementComponent* ProjectileMovement as VisibleAnywhere UPROPERTY so they serialize and are accessible in the editor. Then declare UFUNCTION handlers with the correct signatures for overlap and hit: OnOverlapBegin and OnHit. These signatures are specific: overlaps receive a bFromSweep boolean and an FHitResult for sweep data, while hits receive a NormalImpulse and a const FHitResult& describing contact details. Declaring them with UFUNCTION enables AddDynamic binding later. This header establishes the contract between engine delegates and your methods, ensuring the compiler and runtime know how to call your handlers. A common oversight is using the wrong parameter types — match signatures exactly to avoid binding failures. keyIdea.text: Declare components and UFUNCTION handlers with exact signatures to enable AddDynamic binding for overlap and hit delegates.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Header: Declare components & handlers
Ensure declarations are visible and signatures match engine delegates.
// MyProjectile.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyProjectile.generated.h"

class USphereComponent;
class UProjectileMovementComponent;

UCLASS()
class YOURGAME_API AMyProjectile : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyProjectile();

protected:
    virtual void BeginPlay() override;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Components")
    USphereComponent* CollisionSphere;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Components")
    UProjectileMovementComponent* ProjectileMovement;

    UFUNCTION()
    void OnOverlapBegin(UPrimitiveComponent* OverlappedComp, AActor* OtherActor,
        UPrimitiveComponent* OtherComp, int32 OtherBodyIndex, bool bFromSweep,
        const FHitResult& SweepResult);

    UFUNCTION()
    void OnHit(UPrimitiveComponent* HitComp, AActor* OtherActor, UPrimitiveComponent* OtherComp,
        FVector NormalImpulse, const FHitResult& Hit);
};
Explanation

Make component pointers UPROPERTY so the editor can display and manage them. The UFUNCTION handlers must match the engine delegate signatures exactly to bind with AddDynamic in the constructor.

Concrete example
This header prepares a projectile that will both overlap pickups and hit walls. The two handlers let you separate logic for entering a pickup zone and colliding with static geometry.
Pro tip
Keep handler logic small: log an event and call a helper method. Large logic in the callback can be harder to test.
Key Takeaway

Header declarations form the contract for delegate binding. Match signatures and expose components with UPROPERTY.

screens.title: Constructor & Binding — Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: In the constructor you create component subobjects, set the collision profile or configure individual responses, enable overlap and hit flags, and bind delegates using AddDynamic. Code Walkthrough
Constructor & Binding
Create components, enable flags, and bind event delegates.
// MyProjectile.cpp (constructor excerpt)
AMyProjectile::AMyProjectile()
{
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;

    CollisionSphere = CreateDefaultSubobject<USphereComponent>(TEXT("CollisionSphere"));
    RootComponent = CollisionSphere;

    CollisionSphere->InitSphereRadius(15.0f);
    CollisionSphere->SetCollisionProfileName(TEXT("Projectile"));

    CollisionSphere->SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true);
    CollisionSphere->SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true);

    CollisionSphere->OnComponentBeginOverlap.AddDynamic(this, &AMyProjectile::OnOverlapBegin);
    CollisionSphere->OnComponentHit.AddDynamic(this, &AMyProjectile::OnHit);

    ProjectileMovement = CreateDefaultSubobject<UProjectileMovementComponent>(TEXT("ProjectileMovement"));
    ProjectileMovement->UpdatedComponent = CollisionSphere;
    ProjectileMovement->InitialSpeed = 3000.f;
    ProjectileMovement->MaxSpeed = 3000.f;
    ProjectileMovement->bRotationFollowsVelocity = true;
    ProjectileMovement->bShouldBounce = true;
    ProjectileMovement->Bounciness = 0.3f;
}
Explanation

SetCollisionProfileName applies either your custom Projectile profile or a matching built-in profile. The two flags control overlap generation and hit notifications. Binding with AddDynamic registers your UFUNCTIONs so runtime delegates call them automatically.

Concrete scenario
Spawn this projectile from a test actor. When it passes through a pickup volume you will see the overlap log; when it strikes a wall you will see the hit log with impact location.
Debug tip
If bindings don't fire, verify that the function signatures match and that SetGenerateOverlapEvents / SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision were called before binding.

screens.title: Choosing Overlap vs Hit
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between Overlap and Hit comes down to whether you want passage or physical blocking. Overlap is for situations where actors should pass through but still trigger logic — pickups, checkpoints, or zone effects. Hit is for physical impacts where movement is stopped or physics should respond — bullets impacting a wall, objects landing on the ground, or characters bumping into barriers. Consider these examples: a healing zone uses Overlap so players regain health while walking through; a force field that stops movement uses Block and Hit so the player is physically stopped and you can apply reactive logic. Performance also matters: overlap queries can be cheaper when filtered by channel, whereas physics-driven hits may involve costlier simulation. A common mistake is configuring both sides incorrectly — for example, setting the zone to Block will physically stop the player and never generate overlap. Always map your gameplay intent to the response matrix, enable the necessary flags, and test in the editor visualizer. screens.title: Common Mistakes, Performance, and Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Many collision issues result from configuration errors or expensive collision setups. Start debugging by enabling Show → Collision to visually inspect shapes and responses. If an overlap handler never fires, check Generate Overlap Events on both components, ensure object types and responses are compatible, and confirm your function signature matches the expected delegate. If hit events don't fire, verify SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) and that either Simulate Physics is enabled or the object is configured to generate hit notifications. Performance guidance: use simple primitives instead of complex per-triangle collision on dynamic actors, and apply collision filtering via channels to reduce unnecessary checks. Large numbers of overlapping shapes or per-frame expensive traces cause runtime cost; consider coarse collision for broad checks and finer traces only when needed. When performance is a concern, profile collision queries and reduce the number of components with active collision each frame. Finally, use UE_LOG in your handlers to print diagnostic messages and confirm which actor and component names are arriving at runtime. Process Flow
Debugging & Performance
A practical checklist to find and fix collision issues.

Prefer simplified collision shapes or custom simplified collision meshes for static geometry. Filter by channel to avoid unnecessary overlap checks.
Investigation example
If overlaps never fire, check both the trigger and the pawn capsule's Generate Overlap Events, and use the collision visualizer to confirm shapes actually intersect.
Common misconfigurations
  • Using per-poly collision for many moving objects.
  • Setting responses to Ignore for a channel you expect to interact with.
  • Binding delegates before enabling the required flags.

Correct configuration prevents silent failures and keeps your game responsive. Debug visually and with log messages to find the root cause quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Collision is the foundation of interactive gameplay: it defines when actors meet, when triggers fire, and when physics reacts. In this lesson you will learn the building blocks that Unreal Engine 5 provides — simple geometric primitives for collision, collision presets and channels that filter interactions, and the two event families you use in C++: overlap and hit events. We'll also show a practical projectile example that binds OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentHit so your game can respond to triggers and physical impacts. Understanding the difference between overlap and hit matters because choosing the wrong one leads to missed events or unexpected blocking. For example, trigger volumes use overlaps so players pass through while pickups still register; walls use blocking and hits so movement is stopped and impact logic runs. By the end of this chapter you will know how to configure a component's object type and responses, enable the right event flags, and bind UFUNCTION handlers safely. Keep an eye on performance: simple shapes and smart filtering are essential. Ready to explore collision presets, event binding, and test workflows in the editor?

In this chapter you will gain four practical competencies that connect configuration in the editor with runtime C++ behavior. First, you'll understand collision primitives and presets so you can choose efficient shapes and a preset that matches your gameplay intent. Second, you'll be able to create and configure custom collision channels and object types so different classes of actors interact only the way you intend. Third, you'll implement overlap and hit handlers in C++ using AddDynamic and UFUNCTION so your actors respond to events reliably. Fourth, you'll identify common mistakes such as disabled Generate Overlap Events or incorrect response settings, and learn performance-minded choices like using simple collision or filtering by channel. Each objective includes why it matters and an example: for instance, recognizing that pickups should use overlap events avoids unintended blocking that ruins player movement. These skills will let you design predictable interactions, optimize collision checks, and debug issues in the editor and log output.

This second objectives slide places emphasis on practical verification and testing steps you will perform. You will learn to set collision profile names and test them in the editor by enabling show collision visualizations. You will practice creating a Projectile profile and configuring responses so that projectiles block static world geometry while overlapping pickups. You will also test event binding by spawning a projectile and verifying Output Log messages from your OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentHit handlers. Finally, you will learn to use Generate Overlap Events and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision flags correctly so events actually fire. These verification steps ensure that your configuration matches gameplay intent: triggers detect entry without stopping movement, and blocked collisions produce contact responses. The practice focus ties each configuration step to a concrete editor action and a runtime log check, which helps you debug false negatives and fix misconfigured responses.

Collision primitives are the geometric building blocks Unreal uses to detect contact. The most common are spheres, boxes, and capsules, implemented as components such as USphereComponent, UBoxComponent, and UCapsuleComponent derived from UPrimitiveComponent. Choosing a primitive is a balance between semantic fit and performance: spheres and capsules give smooth bounds for characters and projectiles, boxes are cheap for static props, and complex per-triangle collision should be avoided unless necessary. A primitive attaches to an actor as a component and becomes the basis for queries and physics responses. When you set a primitive as RootComponent, it defines the actor's collision footprint; when it's a child, it augments a visual mesh for triggers or localized collision. Collision Primitives and UPrimitiveComponent means a collision primitive is a basic geometric component used to test and respond to interactions; prefer simple shapes for performance.. In practical terms, shape types, component attachment, and why shape choice matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Collision presets and channels form a matrix that determines how two components interact. A Collision Preset is a convenient predefined set of responses such as BlockAll or OverlapAll. Under the hood, each component has an Object Type and a set of responses to other channels. Collision Channels are categories you define in Project Settings; they represent semantic groups like Pawn, Projectile, WorldStatic, or Pickup. For every pair of object types the engine consults the response (Ignore, Overlap, or Block) and either performs physics, generates overlap events, or ignores the other component. This filtering is essential for performance: well-chosen channels reduce unnecessary queries and ensure only meaningful interactions are processed. For example, you can set your Projectile channel to block WorldStatic and overlap Pickup so projectiles stop at walls but pick up items when passing through. Misconfiguring responses — such as setting both sides to Ignore or both to Overlap when you need a physical block — results in missing events or unexpected pass-through behavior. Always verify both the component's Object Type and its responses in the Details panel. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Overlap events are used when actors should pass through each other while still triggering logic. They occur when components' responses to each other are set to Overlap and at least one side has Generate Overlap Events enabled. This makes overlaps ideal for trigger volumes, pickups, and zone detection. The typical process is: define a trigger component (UBoxComponent or USphereComponent), set its Object Type and Response to Overlap the target Object Type, enable Generate Overlap Events, and bind OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentEndOverlap to UFUNCTION handlers in your actor. Hit events happen when two collision primitives physically collide and are prevented from passing through each other. They are used for impacts, projectile impacts, and physical responses like applying impulses or spawning effects. For hit events to fire, components must be configured to block each other and either simulate physics or explicitly enable Generate Hit Events / SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision. If a rigidbody is involved, Simulate Physics can trigger hits; for static or kinematic objects, SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) is often required. Choose the response according to whether you want a physical block or a trigger-like notification.
